question: In cavernous sinus thrombosis (CST), bilateral proptosis and ophthalmoplegia develop because infection spreads through the circular sinus connecting both cavernous sinuses.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This is true. Bilateral proptosis and ophthalmoplegia in CST occur because infection crosses from one cavernous sinus to the other via the intercavernous sinus (part of the circular sinus). This explains why unilateral facial infection can produce bilateral ocular signs — a key diagnostic red flag for CST vs orbital cellulitis.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. The cavernous sinuses communicate with each other via the intercavernous (circular) sinuses anteriorly and posteriorly. Once septic thrombosis propagates through this communication, bilateral involvement of the contents of the cavernous sinus — CN III, IV, V1, V2, and VI — produces the hallmark bilateral proptosis and ophthalmoplegia of CST. This bilateral spread distinguishes CST from unilateral orbital cellulitis (Chandler V is CST).
